Doses of unfractionated heparin and oral anticoagulants must be adjusted according to laboratory monitoring. In the initial treatment of DVT, unfractionated heparin is giv- en intravenously, as a loading dose of 5000 units, and then continuous infusion at a dose of 18 units/kg per hour, ad- justed according to response;9,56 doses are usually in the range of 1000 to 2000 units/hour. Alternatively, the infu- sion may be replaced with a similar total daily dose given subcutaneously in 2 divided doses;9 in the USA, an initial dose of 17 500 units subcutaneously every 12 hours is rec- ommended.56 However, low-molecular-weight heparins have a number of advantages and are now generally pre- ferred.9,56 A number of meta-analyses58,59 have shown them to be at least as effective and safe as unfractionated heparin in the treatment of deep-vein thrombosis and pul- monary embolism, and a systematic review60 has found that once daily treatment may be as safe and effective as twice daily treatment. They are also safe and effective for the outpatient treatment of DVT61,62 and have been recom- mended for outpatient treatment in patients with uncom- plicated pulmonary embolism.6 Fondaparinux has been reported63 to be an effective alter- native to low-molecular-weight heparin in the initial treat- ment of venous thromboembolism. Ancrod, argatroban, or the recombinant hirudin, lepirudin, may be used as an al- ternative to heparin in patients who have developed heparin-induced thrombocytopenia or thrombosis. A heparinoid such as danaparoid or a low-molecular-weight heparin may also be suitable, although there may be cross- reactivity. Treatment with an oral anticoagulant (usually warfarin) should generally be started at the same time as heparin.56 A standard loading dose is usually given, and dosage is then adjusted to maintain the INR within recommended limits.56,64 Heparin should be continued until the INR is stable and in the therapeutic range;56 5 to 7 days is usually adequate. The optimum duration of oral anticoagulation is unclear. Meta-analyses65,66 of studies comparing different lengths of treatment have found that recurrence is reduced for as long as anticoagulation is continued; therefore, to prevent recurrence, treatment should ideally be continued for as long as the patient is at risk.
